content: Wittenoom is a location situated in the Pilbara region of Western Australia, approximately 1,106 kilometers north-northeast of Perth. In the 1950s, it was the largest town in the Pilbara region. However, it was closed in 1966 due to significant health concerns arising from asbestos mining activities in the nearby Wittenoom Gorge. Today, Wittenoom is classified as a ghost town, with only about eight residents remaining. These residents do not receive any government services. In December 2006, the Government of Western Australia announced its decision to officially degazette the town. By June 2007, the townsite status of Wittenoom was formally removed, as declared by Hon. Jon Ford, the Minister for Regional Development. Consequently, the town's name was removed from official maps and road signs. The Shire of Ashburton was also granted the authority to close roads leading to areas contaminated by asbestos. A report conducted in 2006 by independent geotechnical consultants, and later reviewed by the Department of Health, confirmed that the levels of asbestos fibers in Wittenoom posed an unacceptable public health risk. The town of Wittenoom was named by Lang Hancock after Frank Wittenoom (1855–1939), who was his partner in the nearby Mulga Downs Station. The land surrounding Wittenoom was originally settled by Frank Wittenoom's brother, Sir Edward Horne Wittenoom, a politician. Lang Hancock discovered Wittenoom Gorge in the early 1930s and began mining blue asbestos (crocidolite) there in 1937. In 1943, the mine was sold to a subsidiary of CSR Limited, Australian Blue Asbestos Pty Ltd. By the late 1940s, the need for a nearby townsite to accommodate mine workers and their families became apparent, and the town was officially gazetted in 1950. In 1951, CSR requested the town's name be changed to Wittenoom Gorge, but it was reverted to Wittenoom in 1974. Between 1950 and the early 1960s, Wittenoom was Australia's sole supplier of asbestos, with 161,000 tonnes mined during this period. Over 20,000 men, women, and children lived and worked in Wittenoom during its operational years. Since then, more than 1,000 individuals have died from asbestos-related diseases, including asbestosis, lung cancer, and mesothelioma. The National Health and Medical Research Council estimates that the eventual death toll will exceed 2,000. Despite the ongoing risks associated with airborne asbestos fibers, a small number of residents continued to live in Wittenoom as of early 2006, defying the Western Australian Government's removal of services and stated intention to demolish the town. On June 30, 2006, the government disconnected Wittenoom from the power grid. Between May and November 2006, three residents accepted the government's offer to purchase their homes for up to A$39,804, along with a 10% solatium and A$10,000 for relocation costs. In December 2006, Jon Ford, the Minister for the Pilbara and Regional Development, announced that Wittenoom's status as a town would be officially removed. By June 2007, this status was formally revoked. Ford encouraged the remaining residents to accept the government's relocation offer, citing a detailed report on asbestos contamination in Wittenoom that classified the risks for most categories of people using the sites in and around the town as medium to high. The Western Australian Department of Health reviewed the report and concluded that the levels of contamination exposure in Wittenoom represented an unacceptable public health risk. A Steering Committee, comprising representatives from various government departments, meets regularly to oversee the ongoing closure of the area. Wittenoom is located near several stunning gorges in the Hamersley Ranges and Karijini National Park. The town and its mining history inspired the Midnight Oil song Blue Sky Mine, as well as He Fades Away and Blue Murder by Alistair Hulett.
